 The best home battery for backup power is the one whose continuous output (kW) covers the loads you run at the same time and whose capacity (kWh) covers the hours you want to ride through. Among the batteries we reviewed, the Tesla Powerwall 3 and FranklinWH aPower 2 offer the highest output from a single unit, and Enphase IQ Batteries are the most modular. All figures below come from manufacturer documents or the published analyses we name, as of October 24, 2026.
 We have not tested these batteries. Our picks rest on specs, certifications, warranties and published expert and installer-marketplace analyses. See how we pick products .
 Quick picks
 Best for Pick Capacity Continuous power Warranty 
 Most output from one unit Tesla Powerwall 3 13.5 kWh (nominal) 11.5 kW 10 years 
 Largest single-unit capacity, rugged outdoor install FranklinWH aPower 2 15 kWh 10 kW 15 years / 60 MWh 
 Midsize modular backup Enphase IQ Battery 10C 10 kWh 7.08 kW 15 years / 6,000 cycles 
 Starting small, adding later Enphase IQ Battery 5P 5.0 kWh 3.84 kW 15 years / 6,000 cycles 
 Sources: Tesla Powerwall 3 datasheet (nominal energy; the datasheet does not state usable energy), FranklinWH aPower 2 product page (15 kWh stated without specifying usable), Enphase IQ Battery 10C and IQ Battery 5P .
 What does a backup battery actually have to do?
 Two numbers decide backup performance:
 Power (kW): the most the battery can deliver at one moment. Add up everything that might run together: refrigerator, lights, internet, well pump, furnace blower, an air conditioner.
 Energy (kWh): how long that power lasts. Hours of backup = usable kWh ÷ average kW load.
 Example (an illustration with assumed numbers, not a measurement): a home that averages 1.5 kW of essential loads for a 12-hour overnight outage needs 1.5 × 12 = 18 kWh. One 13.5 kWh battery would run out in about 9 hours (13.5 ÷ 1.5) before any solar recharge. See how to size a home battery for the full method, and our earlier battery sizing guide for a lighter-load example.
 Product cards
 Tesla Powerwall 3 — best for high output from one unit
 Tesla’s datasheet lists 13.5 kWh nominal energy, 11.5 kW maximum continuous discharge, a 10-year warranty, an operating range of -4°F to 122°F (derating possible above 104°F) and up to 20 kW of solar input across six MPPTs. It lists UL 1741, UL 9540, UL 9540A and UL 1973 among its certifications. Tesla’s own product page says it includes an integrated solar inverter.
 Pros 
 Highest continuous output of the batteries we compared.
 Integrated inverter means one box can handle solar and storage in a new install.
 Broad UL certification list on the datasheet.
 Cons 
 Shortest warranty of the four (10 years).
 Datasheet states nominal, not usable, energy.
 Tesla’s public pages do not list a price; installed cost varies by installer.
 Approximate price: EnergySage’s April 2026 battery ranking lists $998 per kWh; Solar.com’s battery guide reports a median of about $15,000 installed with solar (September 2026 installer price lists, before incentives). Prices checked October 24, 2026.
 Check price 
 FranklinWH aPower 2 — best for capacity and tough sites
 FranklinWH’s product page lists 15 kWh capacity, 10 kW continuous power, a 15-year warranty covering 60 MWh of throughput, IP67 dust and water protection, LFP chemistry and an operating range of -4°F to 131°F. It says up to 15 units can stack per aGate controller. The page does not state peak power or a UL 9540 listing, so ask your installer for the certification documents.
 Pros 
 Largest single-unit capacity here.
 Long warranty and an IP67 rating.
 FranklinWH says a single unit can start a 5-ton air conditioner.
 Cons 
 Certifications are not stated on the product page we read.
 The page does not say whether 15 kWh is usable energy.
 Uses FranklinWH’s own aGate controller, so it is a different ecosystem from Tesla or Enphase.
 Approximate price: EnergySage lists $1,177 per kWh; Solar.com reports about $17,250 median installed with solar (before incentives). Prices checked October 24, 2026.
 Check price 
 Enphase IQ Battery 10C — best for midsize modular backup
 Enphase’s product page lists 10 kWh, 7.08 kW continuous power and a 15-year warranty covering up to 6,000 cycles. It cites UL 9540A certification. A third-party comparison from NuWatt Energy describes it as AC-coupled and best suited to homes already using Enphase microinverters; we did not confirm the coupling on Enphase’s own page.
 Pros 
 Long warranty for the capacity.
 Modular: more units can be added.
 Natural fit with Enphase microinverter systems.
 Cons 
 Lower continuous power than a single Powerwall 3 or aPower 2.
 The Enphase page does not state operating temperature.
 Highest per-kWh price among the batteries EnergySage ranks here (see below).
 Approximate price: EnergySage lists $1,404 per kWh; Solar.com reports about $14,250 median installed with solar. Prices checked October 24, 2026.
 Check price 
 Enphase IQ Battery 5P — best for starting small
 The IQ Battery 5P lists 5.0 kWh usable capacity, 3.84 kW continuous power, 7.68 kW peak for 3 seconds and 6.14 kW for 10 seconds, six embedded grid-forming microinverters and a 15-year warranty up to 6,000 cycles. Backup requires an IQ System Controller 3 or 3G, and commissioning requires an Enphase-certified installer.
 Pros 
 Small steps: add units as budget allows.
 Enphase states usable (not nominal) capacity.
 Cons 
 You may need several units for whole-home backup, and the controller adds cost.
 Solar.com’s median for a no-backup version is about $6,125, but about $10,650 with backup, so the backup hardware matters.
 Check price 
 What about owner reviews?
 We looked for large, independent owner-satisfaction data on the batteries themselves and did not find a source we trust. Solar.com’s analysis covered 158,781 Google and Yelp reviews of California solar installers, 8,124 of which mention a battery, but it says those ratings reflect installer performance, not battery quality. Treat installer reputation as its own decision, and see how to compare solar quotes .
 Who should skip a battery
 Outages are rare and short. A battery is expensive insurance. If you mostly need to keep a phone, router and refrigerator going, a smaller system, or no battery, may do.
 You are on a flat rate with generous net metering. A battery adds little bill savings there. See net metering by state .
 You plan to run a large well pump or central air for days. Batteries ride through outages; they do not replace a generator for multi-day events unless sized and recharged by solar.
 You expect a federal tax credit. The credit for batteries placed in service after December 31, 2025 has ended (below).
 Incentives: what changed
 The IRS says the residential clean energy credit is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025. Storage of at least 3 kWh used to qualify. State incentives, utility battery programs and different rules for leased systems may still apply. Check your state’s page in Rates by State and ask your installer for the written basis of any incentive they quote. Confirm eligibility with a qualified tax professional.
 Buying checklist
 Critical loads and their kW. List what must run at once, including starting surges.
 Hours of backup. Hours = usable kWh ÷ average kW.
 Existing solar. Same-brand microinverters or a new hybrid system change which battery fits.
 Budget at full price. Get at least three written quotes with equipment model numbers.
 Climate and location. Compare operating temperature ranges and outdoor ratings.
 Warranty. Compare years and any cycle or throughput cap.
 Utility rules. Interconnection approval and export rules vary by utility; see our rate and policy guides .
 Certifications. Ask for UL 9540 documentation for the exact model.
 Limitations
 Figures are manufacturer-stated, sometimes nominal rather than usable, and prices are approximate installed medians or per-kWh figures from marketplaces, not quotes. Prices vary by home, utility and installer. This is not tax or engineering advice.

 What is the best home battery for backup power?
 For a single unit that can carry most of a home, the Tesla Powerwall 3 (11.5 kW continuous, 13.5 kWh nominal) and FranklinWH aPower 2 (10 kW continuous, 15 kWh) have the highest output of the batteries we reviewed. Enphase IQ Batteries are better when you want to add capacity in small steps or already have Enphase microinverters.
 How many batteries do I need to back up a whole house?
 It depends on the loads you want to run at once (kW) and for how long (kWh). Add up the loads, divide your target energy by one battery's capacity and round up. Our battery sizing guide walks through the formula.
 Is there still a federal tax credit for home batteries?
 The IRS says the residential clean energy credit is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025. State, local and utility programs may still apply. Confirm eligibility with a qualified tax professional.
 Can a home battery run central air conditioning?
 Sometimes. Starting a compressor needs a short surge well above its running power. Tesla's datasheet lists the ability to start loads up to 185 LRA, and FranklinWH says the aPower 2 can start a 5-ton A/C. Confirm your specific unit's starting current with your installer.

Best Whole-Home Batteries 2026: Powerwall vs Franklin vs Enphase vs EG4 | Own Your Electricity 
 🛒 Disclosure: This article contains affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Learn more .
 Quick Answer: For most homes in 2026, the Tesla Powerwall 3 is the best all-around whole-home battery. It offers 13.5 kWh usable capacity and 11.5 kW continuous output. FranklinWH aPower 2 handles larger motor loads. Enphase 5P fits existing Enphase solar. EG4 PowerPro costs less per kWh but requires more installation planning.
 Table of Contents 
 Whole-home batteries are no longer a niche upgrade. Extreme weather, time-of-use rates, and grid instability have pushed more homeowners to add storage in 2026. This guide compares four big names: Tesla Powerwall, FranklinWH, Enphase, and EG4. Each brand uses different chemistry, inverter arrangements, and installer channels. The right choice depends on your panel size, solar setup, and whether you want true whole-home backup or just essential circuits. Check our whole-home battery cost guide before you compare quotes. A single battery can run lighting, refrigeration, and a gas furnace, but whole-home backup demands more planning. You also need to decide between AC and DC coupled storage.
 Utility rates remain high, and the federal solar tax credit covers battery storage when the system charges from solar. The U.S. DOE notes that residential batteries listed to UL 9540 are safer and easier to permit. A whole-home battery is not a one-size-fits-all box. Continuous output, surge capacity, and stackability matter more than raw price. Our how to size a home battery guide shows how to add up running watts and motor starting watts. A well pump, sump pump, and AC all have different starting loads. One oversized battery can cost more than your outage savings. One undersized battery will trip when the compressor kicks on.
 We reviewed spec sheets, warranty terms, and typical installed pricing for 2026. We did not accept marketing cycle life claims at face value. Some batteries list huge surge watts but only for milliseconds. Others need proprietary gateways. The table below compares five models, not four, because EG4 sells two very different wall and rack units. Price cells link to current Amazon search listings. Installed costs are higher. A certified electrician will add $2,000 to $6,000 for labor, gateway, and panel work. See how to prepare for power outages if you need a whole-home transfer switch. Motors, well pumps, and electric water heaters add load quickly. Know your loads before picking a battery.
 According to EnergySage , storage hardware prices have fallen, but soft costs still drive final quotes. A battery’s warranty, thermal management, and installer availability can matter more than the spec sheet. We gave extra weight to batteries with UL 9540 listings and clear 10-year warranties. Some readers want a grid-tied battery with solar. Others need an off-grid bank for a cabin. This comparison explains which model fits each use case, and where the hidden costs hide. A cheap battery can become expensive if the inverter, gateway, and labor are not included. Prices below are starting points, not turnkey installed quotes.

 1. Tesla Powerwall 3 , Best all-around AC home battery #

 The Powerwall 3 is the default whole-home battery for a reason. It packs 13.5 kWh of usable LFP cells into one wall unit. Continuous output is 11.5 kW, enough to start most 4-ton air conditioners with a soft start. The integrated inverter removes the need for a separate string inverter, which simplifies new solar installs. Check the Tesla Powerwall 3 on Amazon for current hardware pricing.  The aPower 2 is built for heavy electrical panels. The 13.6 kWh LFP battery delivers 10 kW continuous and handles short surges up to 15 kW. That means a 3-ton AC, a well pump, and a microwave can ride through a transfer without tripping the battery. FranklinWH uses a separate aGate gateway, which manages automatic islanding and transfer. Installers like the aPower 2 because the aGate can stack up to 15 aPower units. You can start with one and add capacity later. The downside is installed price. Most quotes land between $12,000 and $16,000 before incentives. Compare this against a standby generator with our solar battery vs generator guide .  3. Enphase IQ Battery 5P , Existing Enphase solar systems # 
 The IQ Battery 5P is a 5 kWh LFP unit with a 3.84 kW continuous output. That is small. You need at least two or three 5P batteries to back up a normal 200 A panel. The advantage is tight microgrid integration with Enphase IQ8 microinverters. The system forms an island using the IQ System Controller 3. For homes already running Enphase inverters, this is the cleanest path. The Enphase app shows per-panel and per-battery data without third-party middleware. But the cost per kWh is high.  EG4 targets the cost-conscious buyer. The PowerPro WallMount stores 14.3 kWh of LFP cells in a weather-rated enclosure. EG4 sells through distributors and online retailers, but certified installer coverage is thinner than Tesla or Enphase. You may need to coordinate electrical work yourself.  5. EG4 PowerPro Indoor , Indoor rack or basement battery bank # 
 The indoor PowerPro uses the same 14.3 kWh LFP cell block but in a non-weatherized enclosure. It is designed for a basement, garage, or utility room. Because it is indoor only, it costs slightly less than the outdoor WallMount. You can parallel multiple units to build a 28.6 kWh or 42.9 kWh bank. Plan for DC cables, disconnects, and the inverter. This is not a plug-and-play AC battery. Your electrician must install overcurrent protection and a UL 9540 listed energy storage system. The PowerPro Indoor pairs well with an EG4 18kPV or a Schneider XW Pro.
 Key strengths: 
 ✅ 14.3 kWh LFP capacity at a lower price than the outdoor model
 ✅ Parallels easily for 28.6 kWh or larger banks
 ✅ Works with multiple hybrid inverter brands
 ✅ 10-year warranty
 ❌ Indoor-only installation limits placement
 ❌ Requires a compatible hybrid inverter and separate wiring
 ❌ No integrated gateway or smart app from EG4
 Who it’s for: Homeowners with a dedicated utility room or basement who want a low-cost indoor battery bank.
 Frequently Asked Questions # 
 What is the best whole-home battery in 2026? 
 For most homes, the Tesla Powerwall 3 is the best all-around choice because it pairs 13.5 kWh of usable capacity with 11.5 kW continuous output. FranklinWH aPower 2 is better for heavy motor surges, and EG4 PowerPro is best for cost per kWh.
 How much does a whole-home battery cost installed in 2026? 
 Expect $10,000 to $16,000 for a single battery installed before incentives, including gateway and labor. EG4 systems often start around $8,000 with installation. The federal solar tax credit can reduce the net cost by 30 percent if the system meets requirements.
 Can I install a whole-home battery myself? 
 No. Whole-home batteries involve line voltage, transfer switches, and local code requirements. A licensed electrician must install and inspect the system. DIY electrical work on a service panel is dangerous and may void warranties or insurance.
 Which battery can run a central air conditioner? 
 Tesla Powerwall 3 and FranklinWH aPower 2 can start most 3 to 4 ton central AC units when paired with a soft start. Enphase IQ Battery 5P needs at least two units for motor loads. EG4 PowerPro with an 18kPV inverter handles similar surges.
 Does a whole-home battery qualify for the federal solar tax credit? 
 Yes. The Residential Clean Energy Credit covers battery storage if the system is charged by solar at least 75 percent of the time. Storage-only systems may not qualify. Check the IRS form and your installer’s documentation.
 What does UL 9540 listing mean for a home battery? 
 UL 9540 is a safety standard for energy storage systems and their inverters. Many jurisdictions require it for permit approval. It covers fire, electrical, and thermal safety. Confirm both the battery and inverter are listed as a pair.
 What Should You Remember? # 
 Powerwall 3 capacity: 13.5 kWh usable and 11.5 kW continuous output for whole-home backup.
 FranklinWH surge: aPower 2 delivers 10 kW continuous and 15 kW surge for large motor loads.
 Enphase fit: IQ Battery 5P is best for homes already running Enphase IQ8 microinverters.
 EG4 value: PowerPro batteries offer 14.3 kWh at the lowest cost per kWh among the group.
 UL 9540 listing: Verify the battery and inverter pair is listed before pulling a permit.
 Installed cost: Add $2,000 to $6,000 for gateway, labor, and panel work beyond hardware.
 Sizing first: Use a load calculation before choosing one battery or a stacked bank.
 This article is for general information only. Home energy systems involve high-voltage electrical work, building codes, permits, and in some cases utility interconnection approvals , always consult a licensed electrician and your local authority before making purchase or installation decisions. Product specs, pricing, and incentives (including tax credits and net metering) change frequently; verify current details with the manufacturer and your utility.

 Which home battery is best for you? Our take

 What you need & how it works

 1 New solar + battery install? Go DC-coupled. Sigenergy is the price leader with the best modularity and the lowest future expansion costs. Tesla Powerwall 3 is also excellent — polished, proven, and great value with its integrated 6-MPPT inverter. 
 2 Already have Enphase microinverters? Enphase IQ Batteries are the natural add-on — same app, same monitoring, native integration, plus a 15-year warranty. No new inverter needed. 
 3 Adding battery to an existing non-Enphase solar system? FranklinWH aPower 2 is a strong AC-coupled retrofit — it works with virtually any existing inverter and scales to 225 kWh if you have a large home. 
 4 Do you (or will you) own a compatible EV? New Model 3 / Model Y or Cybertruck? Tesla Powershare with Powerwall 3 lets the car back up your home. Other bidirectional EVs? Sigenergy's V2X works across brands. Either way, your car becomes a 60–100 kWh backup battery that also drives. 
 Frequently asked questions
 What does a home battery cost installed in Southeastern PA? + Installed pricing starts around $15,000 and varies depending on the battery system, storage capacity, electrical panel requirements, and site conditions.  Do all four work with PECO's 1:1 net metering? + Yes. All four are grid-tied capable and fully compatible with PECO net metering. The battery determines what happens during outages and time-of-use arbitrage — net metering is a separate function of the inverter and your interconnection agreement.
 Which has the best warranty? + FranklinWH and Enphase both offer 15-year warranties — FranklinWH's includes a 60 MWh throughput guarantee, which accounts for actual cycling. Tesla and Sigenergy are both 10 years. All four warranty 70%+ usable capacity at end of term.
 Can I mix and match — say, Tesla solar with a Sigenergy battery? + Generally no. Each manufacturer's battery talks to its own inverter and gateway. AC-coupling FranklinWH or Enphase to a different brand's solar inverter is possible; coupling Tesla Powerwall 3 or Sigenergy SigenStor to a third-party solar inverter is more limited because they're hybrid systems designed to manage the solar side themselves.
 Are any of these eligible for incentives? + Pennsylvania does not currently offer state-level battery rebates. The federal 30% residential clean energy credit (IRS) ended December 31, 2025. New Jersey (Jersey Shore service area) has battery incentive programs — those vary by year. We confirm current eligibility during the consultation.
 How long does battery backup last during an outage? + Runtime depends on usable battery capacity, household loads, weather, and available solar charging. For example, 13.5 kWh at a steady 1 kW load is about 13.5 hours before accounting for reserve settings and losses. Heavy loads shorten runtime. Solar or a compatible EV may extend backup, but unlimited or multi-day protection is not guaranteed.

 Powerwall 3 vs Enphase vs FranklinWH: Compare the Whole System
 Tesla Powerwall 3, Enphase IQ Battery and FranklinWH aPower 2 compared on usable kWh, power, installed cost, expansion, warranty and backup design.

 Written by Marcus Reed 
 Reviewed by Home Battery Guide Editorial Team , Editorial review 
 Buyer stage Comparison 
 Comparison 
 Quick answer: Powerwall 3 is the strongest default for a high-power 13.5 kWh single unit and lower installed cost per kWh. Enphase is the modular choice, especially with existing Enphase solar, but several 5P units and the System Controller can make whole-home backup expensive. FranklinWH aPower 2 gives 15 kWh and a strong whole-home design with a longer published warranty, but local certified-installer depth matters.
 Best for
 US homeowners with Tesla, Enphase or FranklinWH battery proposals in hand.
 Wrong fit
 Off-grid systems, portable power stations or buyers comparing only sticker prices without backup scope.
 Tradeoff
 Tesla leads on power and price, Enphase on modular serviceability, and FranklinWH on large-cabinet whole-home design and warranty length.
 Tesla Powerwall 3, Enphase IQ Battery and FranklinWH aPower 2 can all back up a home. They do it with different architectures, and those differences matter more than a brand ranking.
 Powerwall 3 is a large, high-power battery with an integrated solar inverter. Enphase builds capacity in smaller AC-coupled modules. FranklinWH pairs a large 15 kWh cabinet with the required aGate controller. Compare the complete design, not three battery boxes.
 Quick comparison
 Decision Tesla Powerwall 3 Enphase IQ Battery 5P FranklinWH aPower 2 
 Usable capacity 13.5 kWh 5.0 kWh per unit 15 kWh 
 Continuous output 11.5 kW 3.84 kW per unit 10 kW product-page claim 
 Architecture Hybrid inverter with solar inputs AC-coupled, modular AC home-power system with aGate 
 Typical 2026 installed lane About $13,000-$16,500 About $5,500-$6,500 per 5P; backup controller can push one-unit design to $7,500-$9,500 About $15,000-$20,000 with aGate 
 Published warranty 10 years; 70% capacity at year 10 for covered use 15 years or 6,000 cycles on 5P 15 years or 60 MWh, registration required 
 Best fit High power, solar-plus-storage, common ecosystem Existing Enphase solar and staged expansion Larger single cabinet and whole-home control 
 Main quote risk Backup scope, service queue and expansion power Small sticker hides controller and stacked-unit cost aGate and load-management scope buried in one line 
 Pricing is a planning range from July 2026 source checks, before local incentives. It is not a quote. Panel work, backup switchgear, conductor runs, permits and the chosen loads can move any proposal by thousands.
 Powerwall 3: the default high-power value
 One Powerwall 3 provides 13.5 kWh usable capacity and Tesla lists 11.5 kW continuous AC output. That makes a single cabinet unusually capable of starting and carrying larger household loads. Its integrated solar inputs also make it a natural solar-plus-storage proposal.
 The value case is strongest when a certified installer can deliver the complete system near the lower end of the $13,000 to $16,500 planning range. Tesla-direct pricing pulled in early 2026 ran higher in several markets, while marketplace quotes showed that third-party certified installers can be more competitive.
 Expansion units add 13.5 kWh at a lower incremental cost because they share the Powerwall 3 inverter. That adds runtime, not inverter output. If the first cabinet cannot start the proposed load, adding only energy does not solve the power problem.
 Choose Powerwall 3 when: a high-power single unit covers the load plan, the installer and service path are credible, and the quote clearly identifies Backup Gateway or utility-approved Backup Switch scope.
 Watch: a proposal that assumes virtual-power-plant revenue or incentives without current program terms, or a system that depends on internet connectivity without explaining offline backup behavior and warranty requirements.
 Enphase: the modular and serviceable choice
 The IQ Battery 5P stores 5 kWh and provides 3.84 kW continuous output per unit. That smaller module is useful when the homeowner wants to start small, add in 5 kWh increments or stay inside an existing Enphase solar ecosystem. AC coupling also makes retrofit design straightforward in many homes.
 The trap is comparing one $5,500-to-$6,500 installed 5P with a 13.5 or 15 kWh cabinet. Whole-home backup needs enough battery units for both energy and power, plus the IQ System Controller. A one-unit backup-capable design can land closer to $7,500 to $9,500; two and four-unit stacks move the total quickly.
 Enphase's distributed microinverter architecture can be field-serviceable at a module level, and the 5P carries a published 15-year or 6,000-cycle warranty. Confirm generation: older IQ Battery 10 equipment can have different power and warranty terms, while the newer IQ Battery 10C is another current comparison.
 Choose Enphase when: you already own Enphase solar, value staged expansion or serviceable modules, and the stack meets both outage runtime and motor-start needs at a fair complete-system price.
 Watch: a low battery-only line followed later by System Controller, combiner, load control and additional-unit costs.
 Free buyer's guide
 Still deciding between these? Get the straight comparison first.
 What a home battery actually costs, how to read a quote, which backup setup fits your outage, and which incentive claims need dates. Independent. No lead auctions.
 Free. No spam. Unsubscribe whenever.
 FranklinWH: the large-cabinet whole-home choice
 FranklinWH aPower 2 stores 15 kWh and publishes 10 kW continuous output. The required aGate handles backup, load management and system coordination. That makes FranklinWH compelling for buyers who want a whole-home design built around one larger cabinet and explicit load control.
 The planning range is about $15,000 to $20,000 for one aPower 2 with aGate before incentives. Because aGate is required, the first battery carries more control-system cost; additional cabinets can improve the expansion economics.
 FranklinWH publishes a 15-year or 60 MWh warranty for aPower 2. Registration is not paperwork to leave vague: the effective November 2025 end-user warranty states that an unregistered system receives only four years. The local certified installer therefore matters twice - for installation and for preserving the warranty path.
 Choose FranklinWH when: the 15 kWh cabinet and aGate load-control design fit the outage plan and a proven local certified installer will support it.
 Watch: quotes for legacy first-generation aPower at current-product pricing, and proposals that bundle aGate, panel work and load controls so the system cannot be compared line by line.
 Compare equivalent backup, not equivalent kWh
 Before comparing totals, make each bidder mark the same loads:
 HVAC compressor and electric heat strips.
 Well pump, sump pump and septic equipment.
 Refrigerator, freezer and kitchen circuits.
 Medical, office and network loads.
 EV charging and electric water heating.
 Desired outage hours and minimum reserve.
 Then require the continuous power, short-duration motor-start capability, usable energy at the proposed reserve and the load-shedding sequence. A battery can have enough kWh for a long outage but not enough kW to start a motor. The reverse can also happen.
 Use the kWh sizing guide and choose between whole-home and essential-loads backup before allowing a brand to define the scope.
 The quote grid
 Line item Quote A Quote B Quote C 
 Exact battery model and count 
 Usable kWh and continuous kW

 If a line is bundled, ask the contractor to separate it. Use how to read a battery quote before signing.
 Our verdict
 Powerwall 3 is the best starting benchmark for most solar-plus-storage buyers because one cabinet combines 13.5 kWh with high output and competitive installed pricing. Enphase wins when modularity, existing Enphase equipment and field-serviceable architecture are worth stacking smaller units. FranklinWH wins when a 15 kWh cabinet, aGate control and a 15-year registered warranty fit the whole-home plan and local installer depth is strong.
 The best quote is the one that covers the same loads, names every control component and survives a price-per-usable-kWh and price-per-backed-up-load comparison.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is FranklinWH better than Tesla Powerwall 3?
 FranklinWH offers more usable capacity per cabinet and a longer published warranty, while Powerwall 3 offers higher listed continuous output and is often cheaper installed. Local installer support and the complete backup design decide the better system.
 How many Enphase 5P batteries equal one Powerwall 3?
 Three IQ Battery 5P units provide 15 kWh, slightly more energy than one 13.5 kWh Powerwall 3. They also provide 11.52 kW continuous in aggregate. Compare the required System Controller and installation cost, not just the arithmetic.
 Which battery is cheapest per kWh?
 Powerwall 3 is usually the lowest installed-cost-per-kWh benchmark among these three. A real quote can reverse that if Tesla service scope is expensive, an Enphase system reuses existing equipment or FranklinWH expansion shares an existing aGate.
 Which has the best warranty?
 Enphase 5P and FranklinWH publish 15-year terms, with cycle or throughput limits and conditions. Powerwall 3 publishes 10 years with 70 percent capacity retention for covered use. Registration, operating mode, connectivity and labor coverage still need to be read separately. See the home battery warranty guide for the full cross-brand breakdown, including what can void coverage and what happens if the installer closes.

 Methodology
 These guides are built from public specifications, primary program pages, utility documentation, manufacturer materials, and repeated buyer questions that show up in quote and installation decisions.

Best Home Battery Backup Systems 2026: Tested & Ranked | GreenSaveHome

 Disclosure: This post contains Amazon affiliate links. We earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we've tested or thoroughly researched.
 After testing specifications, installation cost data, and user experience reports across every major residential battery system, these are the best home battery backup systems worth buying in 2026 — and the clear category leaders.
 Bottom line up front: The Tesla Powerwall 3 is the best home battery backup for most homeowners (11.5 kW output, 13.5 kWh, $6,650–$8,400 after 30% tax credit). For budget buyers, the Generac PWRcell 9 delivers reliable critical-load coverage for as little as $3,500 after tax credit. For whole-home backup including central AC, two Powerwall 3 units or the FranklinWH aPower 2 are the only real options.
 Quick Picks
 | Use Case | Best Pick | Why |
|----------|-----------|-----|
| Best overall | Tesla Powerwall 3 | Highest power output (11.5 kW), handles central AC, best surge rating |
| Best budget | Generac PWRcell 9 | Lowest cost after tax credit ($3,500–$5,250), great dealer network |
| Best for solar | Enphase IQ Battery 5P | AC-coupled, works with any inverter, modular |
| Best whole-home | 2× Tesla Powerwall 3 | 27 kWh, 23 kW combined — runs everything |
| Best generator pairing | Generac PWRcell 18 | Native integration with Generac standby generators |
 1. Tesla Powerwall 3 — Best Overall
 Specs: 13.5 kWh usable | 11.5 kW continuous | 185A peak surge | 97.5% round-trip efficiency
 The Powerwall 3 is the benchmark every competitor is measured against. Its 11.5 kW continuous output is the highest of any single residential battery unit — enough to run a 3-ton central AC, refrigerator, lights, and miscellaneous loads simultaneously without approaching the power limit.
 The 185A peak surge rating means it reliably starts large compressor motors (AC units, well pumps, refrigerators) that cause most batteries to trip. No other residential battery on the market comes close to this surge capacity.
 What's changed in 2026: Tesla expanded direct-to-consumer installation in 18 additional states, reducing installer dependency. Pricing has remained stable at $9,500–$12,000 installed.
 Best for: Most homeowners wanting whole-home or near-whole-home backup capability, especially in areas with frequent outages or hot summers where AC is critical.
 Not ideal for: Homeowners outside Tesla's installation coverage areas (rural Midwest, rural South), or those with existing Generac generator infrastructure.
 Cost after 30% federal tax credit: $6,650–$8,400 installed
 2. Generac PWRcell 9 — Best Budget Pick
 Specs: 9 kWh usable | 4.5 kW continuous | LFP chemistry | Modular (expandable to 18 kWh)
 At $5,000–$7,500 installed ($3,500–$5,250 after tax credit), the PWRcell 9 is the most affordable path to reliable critical-loads backup from a tier-1 manufacturer. It covers your refrigerator, lights, router, phone chargers, sump pump, and a window AC unit for 12–18 hours on a single charge.
 The 4.5 kW continuous output is the main limitation — it can't run a 3-ton central AC while also powering other loads. But for 80% of homeowners who primarily want to keep food cold, stay connected, and run essential lights during an outage, the PWRcell 9 is entirely sufficient.
 Generator integration is the differentiating feature: if you own a Generac standby generator, the PWRcell communicates with it to minimize generator runtime — the battery handles short outages, the generator starts only for extended events. This hybrid approach is unmatched by any other residential battery system.
 Cost after 30% federal tax credit: $3,500–$5,250 installed
 See our full Generac PWRcell review for detailed specs and real-world performance.
 3. Enphase IQ Battery 5P — Best for Solar Integration
 Specs: 5 kWh usable | 3.84 kW continuous | AC-coupled | Modular (stack multiple units)
 The Enphase IQ Battery 5P is designed for homes with existing solar installations. As an AC-coupled system, it works with any brand of solar inverter — not just Enphase microinverters. That flexibility matters if you're adding storage to an existing SunPower, SolarEdge, or Fronius solar system.
 At 3.84 kW continuous output, a single 5P unit handles all critical loads except central AC. Two units (10 kWh combined) run a 2-ton mini-split comfortably. For whole-home backup with central AC, you'd need three or more units.
 The Enphase ecosystem is best-in-class for monitoring — the Enlighten app shows energy flow to the panel level, with real-time data and detailed historical analytics.
 Best for: Homes with existing solar looking to add storage; homeowners who value detailed monitoring.
 Not ideal for: Non-Enphase installations with whole-home backup goals (power output per dollar is lower than Powerwall 3).
 Cost: $4,000–$6,500 per unit installed before 30% tax credit
 4. FranklinWH aPower 2 — Best Power Output per Dollar
 Specs: 13.6 kWh usable | 12 kW continuous | 200A peak surge | 12-year warranty
 FranklinWH's aPower 2 is the most underrated system in the market. At 12 kW continuous and 200A peak surge, it slightly outperforms the Powerwall 3 on raw power specs — and comes with a 12-year warranty vs. 10 years for most competitors.
 The aPower 2 requires the aGate gateway for grid integration, adding complexity to the installation. It's available through a smaller installer network than Tesla or Generac, but pricing is competitive at $10,000–$14,000 installed.
 Best for: Homeowners in competitive installer markets who want maximum specs; tech-forward buyers who research deeply before purchasing.
 Not ideal for: Those in areas with limited installer coverage; buyers who want the simplest possible installation process.
 5. Generac PWRcell 18 — Best for Whole-Home + Generator Pairing
 Specs: 18 kWh usable | 5.9 kW continuous | LFP chemistry | Expandable
 The PWRcell 18 (6 battery modules) is Generac's whole-home storage solution. The 5.9 kW continuous output handles most mid-size homes without central AC during backup, or works paired with a Generac generator for unlimited runtime on extended outages.
 Where the PWRcell 18 shines is the generator-battery hybrid use case. Homeowners in hurricane-prone states (Florida, Texas Gulf Coast, Carolinas) who already have Generac standby generators can add the PWRcell 18 to create a system where:
 The battery handles day-to-day TOU savings and short outages silently
 The generator starts only for multi-day events
 Total generator fuel consumption drops 60–80%
 Cost after 30% federal tax credit: $6,300–$9,100 installed
 How to Choose
 Step 1: Know your load requirements
 Critical loads only (fridge, lights, router, sump pump): Any system works. Start with the cheapest option — Generac PWRcell 9 or Enphase IQ 5P.
 Add window AC: You need at least 4 kW continuous output. Generac PWRcell 9 (4.5 kW) just handles it; Powerwall 3 (11.5 kW) handles it with room to spare.
 Run central AC during outages: You need 7+ kW continuous output and a high surge rating. Only Tesla Powerwall 3 or FranklinWH aPower 2 qualify as single units.
 Step 2: Consider outage duration
 Under 12 hours: Any 10–14 kWh system covers you without solar.
 12–48 hours: Pair with solar, or size up to 20+ kWh.
 72+ hours / multi-day: You need solar + battery OR a standby generator. A battery-only approach requires very large storage.
 Step 3: Check installer availability
 Tesla is strongest in coastal cities. Generac has the widest dealer network in rural and suburban markets. Enphase installers are everywhere, especially in solar-heavy markets. FranklinWH has more limited coverage — verify dealer availability in your zip code before specifying.
 Step 4: Calculate your net cost
 All home battery systems qualify for the 30% federal tax credit (IRA Section 25D) through 2032. Many states and utilities add additional rebates:
 California SGIP: $200–$1,000/kWh rebate (income-qualified)
 New York Con Edison: $250–$350/kWh incentive
 Massachusetts SMART: Battery adders for solar + storage
 Texas utilities: Various demand response incentives
 Always check your state's DSIRE database (dsireusa.org) for current incentives before finalizing your purchase.

|--------|----------|-----------------|----------------|------------------|----------|
| Enphase IQ 5P | 5 kWh | 3.84 kW | $4,000–$6,500 | $2,800–$4,550 | 10 years |

| Tesla Powerwall 3 | 13.5 kWh | 11.5 kW | $9,500–$12,000 | $6,650–$8,400 | 10 years |
| FranklinWH aPower 2 | 13.6 kWh | 12.0 kW | $10,000–$14,000 | $7,000–$9,800 | 12 years |
| 2× Tesla Powerwall 3 | 27 kWh | 23 kW | $19,000–$24,000 | $13,300–$16,800 | 10 years |
 What to Look For in a Home Battery Backup System (Buying Guide)
 Before committing to any system, evaluate these six specs. Every product in this list was ranked on all six dimensions.
 1. Continuous Power Output (kW)
 This is the most important spec most buyers ignore. Continuous output determines what you can run simultaneously during an outage.
 3–4 kW: Critical loads only (fridge, lights, router, sump pump, phone chargers)
 5–7 kW: Add a window AC unit or small electric water heater
 10–12 kW: Run central AC (3-ton), electric range, or EV charger simultaneously
 20+ kW: True whole-home backup with no load-shedding
 The Tesla Powerwall 3's 11.5 kW and FranklinWH aPower 2's 12 kW are the only single-unit options for central AC backup.
 2. Usable Capacity (kWh)
 Capacity determines how long your backup lasts. Rules of thumb for common loads:
 | Load | Power Draw | Hours on 13.5 kWh Battery |
|------|------------|--------------------------|
| Refrigerator + lights + router | 350W | 38 hours |
| Above + sump pump (intermittent) | 500W avg | 27 hours |
| Above + window AC (1,000W) | 1,500W | 9 hours |
| Above + central AC (3-ton) | 3,500W | 3.9 hours |
 For 24-hour coverage with central AC, you need 27–50 kWh (2–4 battery units).
 3. Battery Chemistry: LFP vs. NMC
 Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP): Safer, longer cycle life (3,000–6,000 cycles), lower energy density. Used in Enphase IQ 5P, Generac PWRcell 2, FranklinWH aPower 2.
 Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC): Higher energy density, slightly better round-trip efficiency. Used in Tesla Powerwall 3.
 For most homeowners, the chemistry difference is minimal. LFP's longer cycle life means Enphase and Generac batteries may outlast their 10-year warranties in actual use.
 4. Round-Trip Efficiency
 How much of the electricity you put in you get back out. Higher is better — lower efficiency means you're "losing" electricity to heat.
 Tesla Powerwall 3: 97.5% (best in class)
 Enphase IQ Battery 5P: 89% 
 Generac PWRcell: 87% 
 FranklinWH aPower 2: 88% 
 A 10% efficiency difference on 250 annual cycles at 13.5 kWh/cycle = 338 kWh lost per year (~$50–$130 in wasted electricity at typical rates). Powerwall 3's higher efficiency advantage compounds over time.
 5. Installer Availability in Your Area
 The best battery on paper is worthless if no installer covers your zip code. Before specifying:
 Tesla: Best coverage in coastal cities, expanding rapidly; check tesla.com/powerwall
 Generac: Widest dealer network, particularly strong in the Midwest and rural South
 Enphase: Ubiquitous with solar installers, available everywhere solar is sold
 FranklinWH: More limited — verify at franklinwh.com/find-installer before deciding
 6. Federal Tax Credit + State Incentives
 All home battery systems qualify for the 30% federal IRA tax credit through 2032, even without solar. Beyond the federal credit, check for state-level programs:
 California SGIP: $200–$1,000/kWh for income-qualified applicants
 New York: Con Edison $250–$350/kWh, NYSERDA rebates
 Massachusetts: SMART program battery adders
 Texas: Various utility demand response programs
 Hawaii: Up to $5,000 state tax credit
 Check dsireusa.org for your state's current database of incentives.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best home battery backup system in 2026? The Tesla Powerwall 3 is the best overall home battery backup in 2026 for most homeowners — 13.5 kWh usable capacity, 11.5 kW continuous power output, and the best surge rating of any residential battery (185A peak). It handles central AC, is widely available, and qualifies for the 30% federal tax credit. For budget buyers, the Generac PWRcell 9 offers solid critical-loads backup for $3,500–$5,250 after tax credit.
 How much does a home battery backup system cost in 2026? Home battery backup systems cost $3,500–$25,000+ installed depending on size. After the 30% federal IRA tax credit: Enphase IQ Battery 5P (5 kWh) runs $3,500–$5,500 installed; Generac PWRcell 9 (9 kWh) runs $3,500–$5,250; Tesla Powerwall 3 (13.5 kWh) runs $6,650–$8,400; two Powerwalls run $13,300–$16,800.
 Do home battery backup systems work without solar panels? Yes. All major home battery systems — Tesla Powerwall 3, Generac PWRcell, Enphase IQ Battery, FranklinWH aPower — charge from the grid and do not require solar panels. Without solar, you're limited to what the battery holds when an outage starts. With solar, the battery recharges each day and extends backup duration indefinitely.
 Which home battery has the longest warranty? Tesla Powerwall 3, Generac PWRcell, and Enphase IQ Battery all carry 10-year warranties with 70% capacity retention. FranklinWH aPower offers a 12-year warranty. All use LFP (lithium iron phosphate) chemistry, which typically lasts 15–20 years in real use before falling below 70% capacity — so the warranty is conservative.
 What is the best battery backup for critical loads only? For critical-loads-only backup (refrigerator, lights, router, phone charging, sump pump), the Enphase IQ Battery 5P (5 kWh, $3,500–$5,500 installed) handles 24+ hours of typical critical loads. The Generac PWRcell 9 (9 kWh) provides more headroom for $3,500–$5,250 after tax credit. Either is appropriate for homeowners who don't need to run central AC during outages.
 What is the best whole home battery backup system? For true whole-home battery backup — including central AC — you need at least 7 kW continuous output and 27+ kWh of storage. The best single-system option is two Tesla Powerwall 3 units stacked (27 kWh, 23 kW combined, $13,300–$16,800 after tax credit). The FranklinWH aPower 2 delivers 12 kW from a single unit at $7,000–$9,800 after tax credit, making it the best value for whole-home power output.
 Which home battery backup system is most reliable? Tesla Powerwall 3 and Enphase IQ Battery 5P consistently rank highest for reliability in independent surveys. Tesla has the largest installed base (over 700,000 units globally) and the best-documented real-world performance. Enphase's LFP chemistry and modular architecture means a single failed unit doesn't take down the whole system. Both carry 10-year warranties with 70% capacity retention guarantees.
 How many kWh do I need for whole-home battery backup? For essential loads only (refrigerator, lights, router, sump pump) for 24 hours, you need 8–12 kWh. To add window AC coverage for 24 hours, plan for 18–24 kWh. For whole-home backup including central AC for 24 hours, you need 30–50 kWh — typically 2–4 battery units. Use this rule of thumb: multiply your daily kWh usage by 0.3 (30%) to cover essential loads for 24 hours.
 Is a home battery backup system worth buying in 2026? Yes, for most homeowners in states with time-of-use electricity rates or frequent outages. After the 30% federal tax credit, a Tesla Powerwall 3 costs $6,650–$8,400 installed and saves $900–$1,250 per year on TOU rates alone — a 5–9 year payback. Add the value of outage protection, reduced generator fuel, and 10-year warranty coverage, and the ROI is compelling in most U.S. markets.

 The best home battery in 2026: Tesla Powerwall 3 (13.5 kWh, ~$12.5–16k), Enphase IQ 5P (modular, 15-yr warranty), FranklinWH aPower 2 (best value), LG RESU Prime. Specs, installed costs, and which battery fits your solar.
 By The PVFig Editorial Team · 2026-08-10 · reviewed against EIA, NREL and DSIRE sources
 The 2026 field, compared
 Tesla Powerwall 3 leads for whole-home backup: 13.5 kWh, 11.5 kW continuous output (runs central AC and EV charging), built-in inverter, ~$12,500–16,200 installed (solarscout/getwattwise 2026), 10-yr warranty. Enphase IQ 5P is the most flexible: 5 kWh per unit, 3.84 kW, ~$6,000–9,000/unit, industry-best 15-yr warranty, works with any solar system. FranklinWH aPower 2 is the value pick: 15 kWh, 10 kW, ~$11,000–20,000, ~$733–1,000/kWh — the lowest cost per kWh of the premium options. LG RESU Prime 16H: 16 kWh, 7 kW, ~$10,000–15,000, safe and widely supported.
 What changed in 2026: no federal credit
 The residential Clean Energy Credit (Section 25D) expired Dec 31 2025 — batteries bought outright in 2026 get no federal credit. The commercial 48E credit still applies to lease/PPA installations (safe harbor for projects beginning construction by July 4 2026), which installers may pass through as lower payments. Overall installed cost in 2026: roughly $10,000–20,000 per unit, or $700–1,300 per kWh (equipment alone $400–850/kWh).
 Which battery fits you
 Backup only: one Enphase IQ 5P ($6,000–12,000, 15-yr warranty). Whole-home backup: Powerwall 3. Time-of-use savings with weak net metering: FranklinWH (stores cheap solar, avoids peak rates). Expandability: Enphase (stack to 20 kWh). Battery economics are strongest where export credits are low (net billing states like CA NEM 3.0) or where time-of-use spreads exceed ~15¢/kWh — a battery can shift $9–15/day of energy.
 FAQ
 What is the best home battery in 2026?
 Tesla Powerwall 3 for whole-home backup (13.5 kWh, 11.5 kW, built-in inverter), Enphase IQ 5P for flexibility and warranty, FranklinWH aPower 2 for best value per kWh (solarscout/13.energy 2026).
 How much does a home battery cost installed in 2026?
 $10,000–$20,000 per unit, or about $700–1,300 per kWh installed. No federal 25D credit applies to 2026 purchases; state incentives (SGIP, ConnectedSolutions) still help.
 Is a home battery worth it without net metering?
 Often yes — in net billing states your exports earn only 3–6¢/kWh while you pay 15–30¢ at night, so a battery that shifts your own solar to evening can pay back in 5–7 years (CA/MA time-of-use markets).
